title: حِكَايَةُ الْبَطَّةِ مَعَ الشِّبْلِ
titleEn: The Duck and the Lion Cub
part: Night 146 · The Duck and the Lion Cub
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 716–724 (Night 146, continuing directly from nights-145), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 146 opens the animal fables Shahriyār asked for. A peacock and his mate, driven from their wooded shore by beasts of prey, settle on an island, where a terrified duck takes refuge with them and tells the peahen her story. A voice in a dream had warned her against the Son of Adam, man, the master of every creature by his tricks. She found a lion cub whose father had warned him of the same enemy, and urged him to kill it. A fleeing donkey, a horse and a camel each tell the cub how man saddles, bridles and works them and sells them to the butcher at last. Then a little old carpenter comes by with his tools and planks, flatters the cub, and offers to build him a house. It turns out to be a box, and once the cub is nailed inside the carpenter throws it in a pit and burns it. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّادِسَةُ وَالْأَرْبَعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sādisatu wa-al-arbaʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the sixth-and-forty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and forty-sixth night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّهُ كَانَ فِي قَدِيمِ الزَّمَانِ وَسَالِفِ الْعَصْرِ وَالْأَوَانِ طَاؤُوسٌ يَأْوِي إِلَى جَانِبِ الْبَحْرِ مَعَ زَوْجَتِهِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu annahu kāna fī qadīmi al-zamāni wa-sālifi al-ʿaṣri wa-al-awāni ṭāʾūsun yaʾwī ilā jānibi al-baḥri maʿa zawjatihi
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that there was, in the olden-part of time and the bygone-part of the age and the season, a peacock (that) took-shelter by the side of the sea with his wife.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that in ancient times and ages long gone there was a peacock who made his home by the seashore with his mate.
sentences.n: A new tale begins, the one the print's running header calls the Tale of the Duck and the Lion Cub (later, the Tale of the Cub and the Carpenter). fī qadīm al-zamān wa-sālif al-ʿaṣr wa-al-awān, “in the olden time and the bygone age and season”: the stock opening of a tale, with zamān and awān rhyming. ṭāʾūs, “peacock”; the hamza on the wāw of طاؤوس is the print's own. awā ilā, “to take shelter in, settle at”, and of birds “to roost”. The birds are called husband and wife (zawja) all through.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ الْمَوْضِعُ كَثِيرَ السِّبَاعِ وَفِيهِ مِنْ سَائِرِ الْوُحُوشِ غَيْرَ أَنَّهُ كَثِيرُ الْأَشْجَارِ وَالْأَنْهَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna dhālika al-mawḍiʿu kathīra al-sibāʿi wa-fīhi min sāʾiri al-wuḥūshi ghayra annahu kathīru al-ashjāri wa-al-anhāri
sentences.l: And that place was much-in beasts-of-prey, and in-it (were some) of all the wild-beasts; except that it (was) much-in trees and rivers.
sentences.i: That place was full of beasts of prey and of every kind of wild creature, though it was rich in trees and streams as well.
sentences.n: sibāʿ (sing. sabuʿ), “beasts of prey”, lions above all; wuḥūsh, “wild beasts”. fīhi min sāʾir al-wuḥūsh, “in it (some) of all the wild beasts”: min means “some of, every sort of”. ghayra annahu, “except that, however”: the trees and waters are the place's good side. The rhyme ashjār / anhār recurs as a pair through the opening.

sentences.t: وَذَلِكَ الطَّاؤُوسُ هُوَ وَزَوْجَتُهُ يَأْوِيَانِ إِلَى شَجَرَةٍ مِنْ تِلْكَ الْأَشْجَارِ لَيْلًا مِنْ خَوْفِهِمَا مِنَ الْوُحُوشِ وَيَغْدُوَانِ فِي طَلَبِ الرِّزْقِ نَهَارًا
sentences.tr: wa-dhālika al-ṭāʾūsu huwa wa-zawjatuhu yaʾwiyāni ilā shajaratin min tilka al-ashjāri laylan min khawfihimā mina al-wuḥūshi wa-yaghduwāni fī ṭalabi al-rizqi nahāran
sentences.l: And that peacock, he and his wife, (they-two) take-shelter in a tree of those trees by-night from their-two fear of the wild-beasts, and (they-two) go-out-at-dawn in search of the provision by-day.
sentences.i: At night the peacock and his mate would roost in one of those trees for fear of the wild beasts, and in the morning they would go out in search of their daily food.
sentences.n: The subject is set at the head and then taken up by dual verbs: “that peacock, he and his wife, they-two roost”. laylan … nahāran, “by night … by day”, balance the two halves. ghadā, “to go out early in the morning”; rizq, “provision, daily bread”, what God allots to each creature.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَالَا كَذَلِكَ حَتَّى كَثُرَ خَوْفُهُمَا فَسَارَا يَبْغِيَانِ مَوْضِعًا غَيْرَ مَوْضِعِهِمَا يَأْوِيَانِ إِلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazālā ka-dhālika ḥattā kathura khawfuhumā fa-sārā yabghiyāni mawḍiʿan ghayra mawḍiʿihimā yaʾwiyāni ilayhi
sentences.l: And they-two did not cease (being) thus until their-two fear grew-great, and they-two set-out seeking a place other-than their place, (that) they-two might-take-shelter in-it.
sentences.i: So they lived until their fear grew too great for them, and they set off to look for some other place where they might find refuge.
sentences.n: lam yazālā ka-dhālika ḥattā, “they did not cease so until”: the stock way of saying “so it went on, until”. baghā, “to seek, desire”. yaʾwiyāni ilayhi, “they would shelter in it”, describes the place they want, with no relative word, as usual after an indefinite noun.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُمَا يُفَتِّشَانِ عَلَى مَوْضِعٍ إِذْ ظَهَرَتْ لَهُمَا جَزِيرَةٌ كَثِيرَةُ الْأَشْجَارِ وَالْأَنْهَارِ فَنَزَلَا فِي تِلْكَ الْجَزِيرَةِ وَأَكَلَا مِنْ أَثْمَارِهَا وَشَرِبَا مِنْ أَنْهَارِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā humā yufattishāni ʿalā mawḍiʿin idh ẓaharat lahumā jazīratun kathīratu al-ashjāri wa-al-anhāri fa-nazalā fī tilka al-jazīrati wa-akalā min athmārihā wa-sharibā min anhārihā
sentences.l: And while they-two (were) searching for a place, lo, there appeared to them an island much-in trees and rivers; and they-two alighted on that island, and ate of its fruits and drank of its rivers.
sentences.i: While they were searching, an island came into view, thick with trees and full of streams. They alighted on it, ate of its fruits and drank of its waters.
sentences.n: fattasha ʿalā, “to search for”, with the colloquial preposition; Classical has fattasha ʿan. baynamā … idh, “while … suddenly”: the stock frame for something that breaks in on an action. athmārihā / anhārihā, “its fruits / its rivers”, close the sentence on a rhyme.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُمَا كَذَلِكَ وَإِذَا بِبَطَّةٍ أَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيْهِمَا وَهِيَ فِي شِدَّةِ الْفَزَعِ وَلَمْ تَزَلْ تَسْعَى حَتَّى أَتَتْ إِلَى الشَّجَرَةِ الَّتِي عَلَيْهَا الطَّاؤُوسُ هُوَ وَزَوْجَتُهُ فَاطْمَأَنَّتْ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā humā ka-dhālika wa-idhā bi-baṭṭatin aqbalat ʿalayhimā wa-hiya fī shiddati al-fazaʿi wa-lam tazal tasʿā ḥattā atat ilā al-shajarati allatī ʿalayhā al-ṭāʾūsu huwa wa-zawjatuhu fa-iṭmaʾannat
sentences.l: And while they-two (were) thus, and behold, a duck came-toward them, and she (was) in the extremity of terror; and she did not cease running until she came to the tree which on-it (were) the peacock, he and his wife; and she grew-calm.
sentences.i: While they were so, a duck came toward them in the utmost terror, and she did not stop running until she reached the tree where the peacock and his mate were perched. There she was at peace.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-baṭṭatin, “and behold, a duck”: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears. baṭṭa, “duck”. saʿā, “to run, hurry along”. iṭmaʾanna, “to be at rest, feel safe”; the hamza in فاطمأنت is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ يَشُكَّ الطَّاؤُوسُ فِي أَنَّ تِلْكَ الْبَطَّةَ لَهَا حِكَايَةٌ عَجِيبَةٌ فَسَأَلَهَا عَنْ حَالِهَا وَعَنْ سَبَبِ خَوْفِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lam yashukka al-ṭāʾūsu fī anna tilka al-baṭṭata lahā ḥikāyatun ʿajībatun fa-saʾalahā ʿan ḥālihā wa-ʿan sababi khawfihā
sentences.l: And the peacock did not doubt that that duck, to-her (was) a wondrous tale; and he asked her about her state and about the cause of her fear.
sentences.i: The peacock had no doubt that there was some strange story behind that duck, and he asked her how she fared and why she was so afraid.
sentences.n: lam yashukka: the jussive of a doubled verb, yashukk, takes a helping vowel, -a. lahā ḥikāyatun, “to her is a tale”: she has a story to tell.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ إِنَّنِي مَرِيضَةٌ مِنَ الْحُزْنِ وَخَوْفِي مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ فَالْحَذَرَ ثُمَّ الْحَذَرَ مِنْ بَنِي آدَمَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat innanī marīḍatun mina al-ḥuzni wa-khawfī mini ibni Ādama fa-al-ḥadhara thumma al-ḥadhara min banī Ādama
sentences.l: And she said: Indeed-I (am) sick from the grief and my fear of the Son of Adam; so (take) the caution, then the caution, of the sons of Adam!
sentences.i: She said, “I am sick with grief and with fear of the Son of Adam. Beware, and beware again, of the sons of Adam!”
sentences.n: ibn Ādam, “the Son of Adam”, and banī Ādam, “the sons of Adam”, are man, humankind, as the animals see him; the phrase runs through the whole tale. al-ḥadhara thumma al-ḥadhara, “caution, then caution!”: the accusative of warning, with “take” or “beware” understood. wa-khawfī is read as joined to al-ḥuzn: sick from grief and from fear.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا الطَّاؤُوسُ لَاتَخَافِي حَيْثُ وَصَلْتِ إِلَيْنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-ṭāʾūsu lā takhāfī ḥaythu waṣalti ilaynā
sentences.l: And the peacock said to her: Do-not-fear, since you have-reached us.
sentences.i: The peacock said to her, “Do not be afraid, now that you have come to us.”
sentences.n: The print runs lā takhāfī together as one word, لاتخافي; the spacing is kept. ḥaythu, “where”, is used here, as in speech, for “since, seeing that”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْبَطَّةُ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي فَرَّجَ عَنِّي هَمِّي وَغَمِّي بِقُرْبِكُمَا وَقَدْ أَتَيْتُ رَاغِبَةً فِي مَوَدَّتِكُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-baṭṭatu al-ḥamdu li-llāhi alladhī farraja ʿannī hammī wa-ghammī bi-qurbikumā wa-qad ataytu rāghibatan fī mawaddatikumā
sentences.l: And the duck said: Praise (be) to God, who has-relieved from-me my care and my grief by your-two nearness; and I have come desiring your-two friendship.
sentences.i: The duck said, “Praise be to God, who has lifted my care and sorrow from me by bringing me near you both. I have come seeking your friendship.”
sentences.n: The print has موتكما, “your death”, a misprint for مودتكما, “your friendship”, corrected here. farraja ʿan, “to relieve someone of (distress)”. hamm wa-ghamm, “care and grief”, a rhyming pair.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَتْ مِنْ كَلَامِهَا نَزَلَتْ إِلَيْهَا زَوْجَةُ الطَّاؤُسِ وَقَالَتْ لَهَا أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا وَمَرْحَبًا لَابَأْسَ عَلَيْكِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghat min kalāmihā nazalat ilayhā zawjatu al-ṭāʾūsi wa-qālat lahā ahlan wa-sahlan wa-marḥaban lā baʾsa ʿalayki
sentences.l: And when she had-finished her speech, the peacock's wife came-down to her and said to her: Family and level-ground and welcome! No harm upon you.
sentences.i: When she had finished speaking, the peacock's mate came down to her and said, “Welcome, and welcome again! You have nothing to fear.
sentences.n: The print spells the word here الطاؤس, with one wāw, beside its usual طاؤوس; both are ṭāʾūs. ahlan wa-sahlan wa-marḥaban, the triple greeting: “(you have come to) family, (you tread) level ground, (you are) welcome”. lā baʾsa ʿalayki, “no harm upon you”, that is, “you are safe”; the print runs it together as لاباس and writes baʾs without its hamza.

sentences.t: وَمِنْ أَيْنَ يَصِلُ إِلَيْنَا ابْنُ آدَمَ وَنَحْنُ فِي تِلْكَ الْجَزِيرَةِ الَّتِي فِي وَسَطِ الْبَحْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-min ayna yaṣilu ilaynā ibnu Ādama wa-naḥnu fī tilka al-jazīrati allatī fī wasaṭi al-baḥri
sentences.l: And from where (could) the Son of Adam reach us, and we (are) in that island which (is) in the middle of the sea?
sentences.i: How could the Son of Adam reach us, when we are on an island in the midst of the sea?
sentences.n: tilka al-jazīra, “that island”, where “this island” is meant: the narrator's word slips into the peahen's speech. wa-naḥnu, “and we …”: a circumstantial clause, “when we are …”.

sentences.t: فَمِنَ الْبَرِّ لَا يَقْدِرُ أَنْ يَصِلَ إِلَيْنَا وَمِنَ الْبَحْرِ لَا يُمْكِنُ أَنْ يَطْلُعَ عَلَيْنَا فَأَبْشِرِي وَحَدِّثِينَا بِالَّذِى نَزَلَ بِكِ وَاعْتَرَاكِ مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ
sentences.tr: fa-mina al-barri lā yaqdiru an yaṣila ilaynā wa-mina al-baḥri lā yumkinu an yaṭluʿa ʿalaynā fa-abshirī wa-ḥaddithīnā bi-alladhī nazala biki wa-iʿtarāki mini ibni Ādama
sentences.l: For from the land he cannot reach us, and from the sea it is not possible that he come-up upon us. So rejoice, and tell-us of-that-which befell you and came-upon you from the Son of Adam.
sentences.i: By land he cannot reach us, and by sea he has no way to come at us. So take heart, and tell us what has befallen you and what has come upon you from the Son of Adam.”
sentences.n: The two clauses rhyme: yaṣila ilaynā / yaṭluʿa ʿalaynā. abshirī, “receive good tidings”, is “cheer up, take heart”. nazala bi-, “to befall”; iʿtarā, “to come upon, seize”, of a trouble or a feeling. The print writes al-ladhī with final ى.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْبَطَّةُ اعْلَمِي أَيَّتُهَا الطَّاؤُسَةُ أَنَّنِي فِي هَذِهِ الْجَزِيرَةِ طُولَ عُمْرِي آمِنَةٌ لَاأَرَى مَكْرُوهًا
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-baṭṭatu iʿlamī ayyatuhā al-ṭāʾūsatu annanī fī hādhihi al-jazīrati ṭūla ʿumrī āminatun lā arā makrūhan
sentences.l: And the duck said: Know, O peahen, that I (have been) in this island the length of my life, safe, not-seeing a hateful-thing.
sentences.i: The duck said: Know, O peahen, that all my life I lived safe on this island and never met with harm.
sentences.n: al-ṭāʾūsa, “peahen”, a feminine made on ṭāʾūs and spelled here with one wāw. The duck has only just arrived, yet speaks of “this island” as her lifelong home; the story is loose here. makrūh, “something hateful”, a misfortune. The print runs lā arā together as لاارى; the spacing is kept.

sentences.t: فَنِمْتُ لَيْلَةً مِنَ اللَّيَالِي فَرَأَيْتُ فِي مَنَامِي صُورَةَ ابْنِ آدَمَ وَهُوَ يُخَاطِبُنِي وَأُخَاطِبُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-nimtu laylatan mina al-layālī fa-raʾaytu fī manāmī ṣūrata ibni Ādama wa-huwa yukhāṭibunī wa-ukhāṭibuhu
sentences.l: And I slept one night of the nights, and I saw in my sleep the form of the Son of Adam, and he (was) addressing me and I addressing him.
sentences.i: Then one night I slept and saw in a dream the figure of the Son of Adam, talking with me as I talked with him.
sentences.n: laylatan mina al-layālī, “a night of the nights”: one night. manām, “sleep”, and so “dream”. ṣūra, “form, image”.

sentences.t: وَسَمِعْتُ قَائِلًا يَقُولُ لِي أَيَّتُهَا الْبَطَّةُ احْذَرِي مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ وَلَا تَغْتَرِّي بِكَلَامِهِ وَلَابِمَا يُدْخِلُهُ عَلَيْكِ فَإِنَّهُ كَثِيرُ الْحِيَلِ وَالْخِدَاعِ
sentences.tr: wa-samiʿtu qāʾilan yaqūlu lī ayyatuhā al-baṭṭatu iḥdharī mini ibni Ādama wa-lā taghtarrī bi-kalāmihi wa-lā bi-mā yudkhiluhu ʿalayki fa-innahu kathīru al-ḥiyali wa-al-khidāʿi
sentences.l: And I heard a speaker saying to me: O duck, beware of the Son of Adam, and do not be-beguiled by his speech, nor by-what he brings-in upon you; for he (is) much-in tricks and deceit.
sentences.i: And I heard a voice say to me, “O duck, beware of the Son of Adam! Do not be taken in by his words, or by anything he works upon you, for he is full of tricks and deceit.
sentences.n: The shadda in تغترّي is the print's. ightarra bi-, “to be beguiled by, trust falsely in”. adkhala ʿalā, “to bring in upon”, here of a trick worked on someone. The print runs wa-lā bi-mā together as ولابما; the spacing is kept. ḥiyal (sing. ḥīla), “tricks, stratagems”.

sentences.t: فَالْحَذَرَ كُلَّ الْحَذَرِ مِنْ مَكْرِهِ فَإِنَّهُ مُخَادِعٌ مَاكِرٌ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهِ الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-al-ḥadhara kulla al-ḥadhari min makrihi fa-innahu mukhādiʿun mākirun kamā qāla fīhi al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: So (take) the caution, all the caution, of his cunning; for he (is) a deceiver, a schemer, as the poet said about him:
sentences.i: Beware, beware with all your might of his cunning, for he is a deceiver and a schemer, as the poet said of him:
sentences.n: makr, “cunning, guile”; mākir, “cunning one”, the participle of the same root. mukhādiʿ, “one who deceives”.

sentences.t: يُعْطِيكَ مِنْ طَرَفِ اللِّسَانِ حَلَاوَةً * وَيَرُوْغُ مِنْكَ كَمَا يَرُوْغُ الثَّعْلَبُ
sentences.tr: yuʿṭīka min ṭarafi al-lisāni ḥalāwatan * wa-yarūghu minka kamā yarūghu al-thaʿlabu
sentences.l: He gives you from the tip of the tongue a sweetness, * and slips-away from you as the fox slips-away.
sentences.i: He offers you sweetness from the tip of his tongue, * then slips away from you as the fox slips away.
sentences.n: ṭaraf al-lisān, “the tip of the tongue”: sweet words that come from no deeper. rāgha, “to dodge, slink off”, the word for a fox's twisting escape. The print marks the long ū of yarūghu with a sukūn on the wāw, يَرُوْغُ, an old habit of pointing; it is kept.

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمِي أَنَّ ابْنَ آدَمَ يَحْتَالُ عَلَى الْحِيتَانِ فَيُخْرِجُهَا مِنَ الْبِحَارِ وَيَرْمِي الطَّيْرَ بِبُنْدُقَةٍ مِنْ طِينٍ وَيُوقِعُ الْفِيلَ بِمَكْرِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlamī anna ibna Ādama yaḥtālu ʿalā al-ḥītāni fa-yukhrijuhā mina al-biḥāri wa-yarmī al-ṭayra bi-bunduqatin min ṭīnin wa-yūqiʿu al-fīla bi-makrihi
sentences.l: And know that the Son of Adam uses-tricks upon the fishes and brings-them-out from the seas, and shoots the birds with a pellet of clay, and makes-fall the elephant by his cunning.
sentences.i: Know too that the Son of Adam outwits the fish and draws them up out of the seas; he shoots down the birds with pellets of clay, and by his cunning he brings down the elephant.
sentences.n: iḥtāla ʿalā, “to use a trick on, outwit”. ḥītān (sing. ḥūt), “fish”. bunduqa, “pellet”: the clay ball shot from a pellet-bow, the bird-hunter's weapon. awqaʿa, “to make fall”, also “to trap”.

sentences.t: وَابْنُ آدَمَ لَا يَسْلَمُ أَحَدٌ مِنْ شَرِّهِ وَلَا يَنْجُو مِنْهُ طَيْرٌ وَلَا وَحْشٌ
sentences.tr: wa-ibnu Ādama lā yaslamu aḥadun min sharrihi wa-lā yanjū minhu ṭayrun wa-lā waḥshun
sentences.l: And the Son of Adam, no one is-safe from his evil, and neither bird nor beast escapes from him.
sentences.i: As for the Son of Adam, no one is safe from his malice, and neither bird nor beast escapes him.”
sentences.n: The Son of Adam is set at the head as the topic, and the clause then speaks of him through “his evil”: a common pattern of spoken Arabic.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ بَلَّغْتُكِ مَا سَمِعْتُهُ عَنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ
sentences.tr: wa-qad ballaghtuki mā samiʿtuhu ʿani ibni Ādama
sentences.l: And I have conveyed-to-you what I heard about the Son of Adam.
sentences.i: Now I have passed on to you what I heard about the Son of Adam.
sentences.n: ballagha, “to convey, pass on (a message)”. The words are most likely the duck's own, closing her report of the dream to the peahen; they could also be the voice's last words to the duck. The sense is the same either way.

sentences.t: فَاسْتَيْقَظْتُ مِنْ مَنَامِي خَائِفَةً مَرْعُوبَةً وَأَنَا إِلَى الْآنَ لَا يَنْشَرِحُ صَدْرِي خَوْفًا عَلَى نَفْسِي مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ لِئَلَّا يَدْهَمَنِي بِحِيلَتِهِ وَيَصِيدَنِي بِحَبَائِلِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-istayqaẓtu min manāmī khāʾifatan marʿūbatan wa-anā ilā al-āna lā yansharihu ṣadrī khawfan ʿalā nafsī mini ibni Ādama liʾallā yadhamanī bi-ḥīlatihi wa-yaṣīdanī bi-ḥabāʾilihi
sentences.l: And I woke from my sleep fearful, terrified; and I, up to now, my breast does not expand, from fear for myself of the Son of Adam, lest he fall-upon-me with his trick and catch-me with his snares.
sentences.i: I woke from my dream afraid and terror-stricken, and to this moment my heart has known no ease, for I fear that the Son of Adam may fall upon me with his tricks and catch me in his snares.
sentences.n: wa-anā … lā yansharihu ṣadrī, “and I, my breast does not expand”: the speaker is set at the head, then her breast becomes the subject. The expanding of the breast is gladness. dahama, “to come upon suddenly”; ḥabāʾil (sing. ḥibāla), “snares, nets”. The hamza in خائفة, الآن, لئلا and بحبائله is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَأْتِ عَلَيَّ آخِرُ النَّهَارِ إِلَّا وَقَدْ ضَعُفَتْ قُوَّتِي وَبَطَلَتْ هِمَّتِي
sentences.tr: wa-lam yaʾti ʿalayya ākhiru al-nahāri illā wa-qad ḍaʿufat quwwatī wa-baṭalat himmatī
sentences.l: And the end of the day did not come upon me except that my strength had weakened and my resolve had come-to-nothing.
sentences.i: Before the day was out my strength had failed and my spirit was spent.
sentences.n: The shaddas in عليّ and الّا are the print's. lam … illā wa-qad, “(it) did not … but that already”: by the time the day ended, this had happened. himma, “resolve, energy”. The print writes yaʾti without its hamza, يات.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنِّي اشْتَقْتُ إِلَى الْأَكْلِ وَالشُّرْبِ فَخَرَجْتُ أَتَمَشَّى وَخَاطِرِي مُكَدَّرٌ وَقَلْبِي مَقْبُوضٌ
sentences.tr: thumma innī ishtaqtu ilā al-akli wa-al-shurbi fa-kharajtu atamashshā wa-khāṭirī mukaddarun wa-qalbī maqbūḍun
sentences.l: Then indeed-I longed for the eating and the drinking, and I went-out walking-about, and my mind (was) troubled and my heart contracted.
sentences.i: Then I began to long for food and drink, and I went out walking, my mind troubled and my heart heavy.
sentences.n: thumma innī, “then I”, literally “then indeed I”, a narrator's filler. tamashshā, “to walk about, stroll”. khāṭir, “mind, mood”; mukaddar, “made muddy”, troubled. qabḍ al-qalb, “the contracting of the heart”, is gloom, the opposite of the expanding of the breast.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلْتُ إِلَى ذَلِكَ الْجَبَلِ وَجَدْتُ عَلَى بَابِ مَغَارَةٍ شِبْلًا أَصْفَرَ اللَّوْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣaltu ilā dhālika al-jabali wajadtu ʿalā bābi maghāratin shiblan aṣfara al-lawni
sentences.l: And when I reached that mountain, I found at the door of a cave a lion-cub yellow of colour.
sentences.i: When I came to that mountain, I found a tawny lion cub at the mouth of a cave.
sentences.n: “That mountain”: no mountain has been mentioned; the storyteller speaks as if the listener knew it. shibl, “lion cub”. aṣfar al-lawn, “yellow of colour”, tawny.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآنِي ذَلِكَ الشِّبْلُ فَرِحَ بِي فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا وَأَعْجَبَهُ لَوْنِي وَكَوْنِي لَطِيفَةَ الذَّاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾānī dhālika al-shiblu fariḥa bī faraḥan shadīdan wa-aʿjabahu lawnī wa-kawnī laṭīfata al-dhāti
sentences.l: And when that cub saw me, he rejoiced in me a strong rejoicing, and there pleased him my colour and my being delicate of person.
sentences.i: When the cub saw me he was overjoyed, and he was taken with my colour and my dainty build.
sentences.n: The print has وكولى, a misprint for وكوني, “and my being”, corrected here. fariḥa … faraḥan shadīdan, “rejoiced a strong rejoicing”: the verb strengthened by its own noun. laṭīfat al-dhāt, “delicate of person, dainty”. The hamza in رآني is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَصَاحَ عَلَيَّ وَقَالَ لِي اقْرَبِي مِنِّي
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāḥa ʿalayya wa-qāla lī iqrabī minnī
sentences.l: And he cried-out to me and said to me: Come-near to me.
sentences.i: He called out to me, “Come close to me.”
sentences.n: The shadda in عليّ is the print's. ṣāḥa ʿalā, “to shout to, call to”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَرِبْتُ مِنْهُ قَالَ لِي مَا اسْمُكِ وَمَا جِنْسُكِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qaribtu minhu qāla lī mā ismuki wa-mā jinsuki
sentences.l: And when I came-near to him, he said to me: What (is) your name, and what (is) your kind?
sentences.i: When I came close, he said to me, “What is your name, and what is your kind?”
sentences.n: jins, “kind, species”.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُ اسْمِي بَطَّةٌ وَأَنَا مِنْ جِنْسِ الطُّيُورِ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahu ismī baṭṭatun wa-anā min jinsi al-ṭuyūri
sentences.l: And I said to him: My name (is) Duck, and I (am) of the kind of the birds.
sentences.i: I said to him, “My name is Duck, and I am of the race of birds.”

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قُلْتُ لَهُ مَا سَبَبُ قُعُودِكَ إِلَى هَذَا الْوَقْتِ فِي هَذَا الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma qultu lahu mā sababu quʿūdika ilā hādhā al-waqti fī hādhā al-makāni
sentences.l: Then I said to him: What (is) the cause of your sitting until this time in this place?
sentences.i: Then I said to him, “Why are you still sitting here in this place at this hour?”
sentences.n: quʿūd, “sitting”, and so “staying, lingering”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الشِّبْلُ سَبَبُ ذَلِكَ أَنَّ وَالِدِى الْأَسَدَ لَهُ أَيَّامٌ وَهُوَ يُحَذِّرُنِي مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-shiblu sababu dhālika anna wālidī al-asada lahu ayyāmun wa-huwa yuḥadhdhirunī mini ibni Ādama
sentences.l: And the cub said: The cause of that (is) that my father the lion, to-him (are) days and he (is) warning me of the Son of Adam.
sentences.i: The cub said, “The reason is that for some days now my father the lion has been warning me against the Son of Adam.
sentences.n: lahu ayyāmun wa-huwa yuḥadhdhirunī, “to him are days, and he warning me”: the spoken way of saying “he has been warning me for days”. The print writes wālidī with final ى.

sentences.t: فَاتَّفَقَ أَنَّنِي رَأَيْتُ فِي هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ فِي مَنَامِي صُورَةَ ابْنِ آدَمَ
sentences.tr: fa-ittafaqa annanī raʾaytu fī hādhihi al-laylati fī manāmī ṣūrata ibni Ādama
sentences.l: And it chanced that I saw in this night in my sleep the form of the Son of Adam.
sentences.i: And it so happened that this past night I saw the figure of the Son of Adam in a dream.”
sentences.n: ittafaqa anna, “it chanced that”. fī hādhihi al-layla, “in this night”: the night just gone.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الشِّبْلَ حَكَى لِي نَظِيرَ مَا حَكَيْتُهُ لَكِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-shibla ḥakā lī naẓīra mā ḥakaytuhu laki
sentences.l: Then the cub told me the like of what I (have) told you.
sentences.i: Then the cub told me a dream like the one I have told you.
sentences.n: naẓīr, “counterpart, the like of”. The duck spares the peahen the repetition, and the storyteller spares the listener.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ كَلَامَهُ قُلْتُ لَهُ يَا أَسَدُ إِنِّي قَدْ لَجَأْتُ إِلَيْكَ فِي أَنْ تَقْتُلَ ابْنَ آدَمَ وَتَحْزِمَ رَأْيَكَ فِي قَتْلِهِ فَإِنِّي أَخَافُ عَلَى نَفْسِي مِنْهُ خَوْفًا شَدِيدًا وَازْدَدْتُ خَوْفًا عَلَى خَوْفِي مِنْ خَوْفِكَ مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ مَعَ أَنَّكَ سُلْطَانُ الْوُحُوشِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿtu kalāmahu qultu lahu yā asadu innī qad lajaʾtu ilayka fī an taqtula ibna Ādama wa-taḥzima raʾyaka fī qatlihi fa-innī akhāfu ʿalā nafsī minhu khawfan shadīdan wa-izdadtu khawfan ʿalā khawfī min khawfika mini ibni Ādama maʿa annaka sulṭānu al-wuḥūshi
sentences.l: And when I heard his speech, I said to him: O lion, indeed I have taken-refuge with you in that you kill the Son of Adam and make-firm your judgement on his killing; for indeed I fear for my soul from him a severe fear, and I increased in fear upon my fear from your fear of the Son of Adam, although you (are) the sultan of the beasts.
sentences.i: When I heard what he said, I told him, “O lion, I have come to you for refuge so that you may kill the Son of Adam and set your mind firmly on his death, for I am terribly afraid of him for my life. And now my fear has grown on top of my fear, seeing that you fear the Son of Adam, though you are the sultan of the beasts.”
sentences.n: The duck is still telling the peahen her story, and here quotes what she said to the lion cub; she addresses him simply as asad, “lion”. lajaʾa ilā, “to take refuge with”; the hamza in لجأت is the print's. ḥazama raʾyahu, “to tie up one's opinion”, to make a firm resolve. khāfa ʿalā nafsihi, “to fear for oneself”. The sentence piles up its key word, khawf, “fear”, four times in one breath: khawfan … khawfan ʿalā khawfī min khawfika.

sentences.t: وَمَا زِلْتُ يَا أُخْتِي أُحَذِّرُ الشِّبْلَ مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ وَأُوصِيهِ بِقَتْلِهِ حَتَّى قَامَ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَسَاعَتِهِ مِنَ الْمَكَانِ الَّذِي كَانَ فِيهِ وَتَمَشَّى وَتَمَشَّيْتُ وَرَاءَهُ فَفَرْقَعَ بِذَنَبِهِ عَلَى ظَهْرِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā ziltu yā ukhtī uḥadhdhiru al-shibla mini ibni Ādama wa-ūṣīhi bi-qatlihi ḥattā qāma min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi mina al-makāni alladhī kāna fīhi wa-tamashshā wa-tamashshaytu warāʾahu fa-farqaʿa bi-dhanabihi ʿalā ẓahrihi
sentences.l: And I did not cease, O my sister, warning the cub against the Son of Adam and charging-him with his killing, until he rose from his time and his hour from the place which he was in, and walked-off, and I walked-off behind him; and he cracked with his tail upon his back.
sentences.i: And I went on, my sister, warning the cub against the Son of Adam and urging him to kill him, until he rose that very moment from the place where he lay and set off walking, and I walked behind him, and he lashed his tail across his back.
sentences.n: yā ukhtī, “O my sister”: the duck turns aside to the peahen she is talking to. mā ziltu + imperfect, “I kept on doing”. awṣā bi-, “to enjoin, urge someone to”. min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi, “from his time and his hour”, a stock phrase for “at once”. tamashshā, “to walk along, stroll”. farqaʿa, “to crack, snap”, of the tail lashing like a whip.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ يَتَمَشَّى وَأَنَا أَمْشِي وَرَاءَهُ إِلَى مَفْرَقِ الطَّرِيقِ فَوَجَدْنَا غَبْرَةً طَارَتْ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal yatamashshā wa-anā amshī warāʾahu ilā mafraqi al-ṭarīqi fa-wajadnā ghabratan ṭārat
sentences.l: And he did not cease walking-along, and I walking behind him, to the parting of the road; and we found a dust (that) flew-up.
sentences.i: He kept on walking, with me walking behind him, as far as the place where the road forks; and there we saw a cloud of dust rise up.
sentences.n: mafraq al-ṭarīq, “the parting of the road”, a crossroads or fork. ghabra, “dust, a cloud of dust”: in these tales a rising dust-cloud always announces someone coming.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ انْكَشَفَتِ الْغَبْرَةُ فَبَانَ مِنْ تَحْتِهَا حِمَارٌ شَارِدٌ عُرْيَانٌ وَهُوَ تَارَةً يَقْمُصُ وَيَجْرِي وَتَارَةً يَتَمَرَّغُ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika inkashafati al-ghabratu fa-bāna min taḥtihā ḥimārun shāridun ʿuryānun wa-huwa tāratan yaqmuṣu wa-yajrī wa-tāratan yatamarraghu
sentences.l: And after that the dust uncovered-itself, and there appeared from under it a donkey, runaway, naked; and he (was) one-time bucking and running and one-time rolling-about.
sentences.i: After a while the dust cleared, and from under it appeared a runaway donkey, bare of saddle and harness, now kicking up his heels and running, now rolling on the ground.
sentences.n: ʿuryān, “naked”, here of an animal with no saddle or gear on it. qamaṣa, “to buck, kick up the heels”. tāratan … wa-tāratan, “at one time … at another”. The shadda in يتمرّغ is the print's.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأٰهُ الْأَسَدُ صَاحَ عَلَيْهِ فَأَتَى إِلَيْهِ خَاضِعًا فَقَالَ لَهُ أَيُّهَا الْحَيَوَانُ الْخَرِيفُ الْعَقْلِ مَا جِنْسُكَ وَمَا سَبَبُ قُدُومِكَ إِلَى هَذَا الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhu al-asadu ṣāḥa ʿalayhi fa-atā ilayhi khāḍiʿan fa-qāla lahu ayyuhā al-ḥayawānu al-kharīfu al-ʿaqli mā jinsuka wa-mā sababu qudūmika ilā hādhā al-makāni
sentences.l: And when the lion saw him, he shouted at him, and he came to him submissive; and he said to him: O you animal, the dotard(?) of mind, what (is) your kind, and what (is) the cause of your coming to this place?
sentences.i: When the lion saw him, he called out to him, and the donkey came up to him meekly. The cub said to him, “You witless creature, what kind of beast are you, and what brings you to this place?”
sentences.n: The print writes رأه for رآه, raʾāhu, “he saw him”, with hamza where the classical spelling has madda; the long ā is shown here by a dagger alif. The cub is called al-asad, “the lion”, from here on as often as al-shibl. ṣāḥa ʿalā, “to shout at, call to”. al-kharīf al-ʿaqli is doubtful: kharīf is “autumn”, which makes no sense here. The likeliest reading is a slip for al-kharif al-ʿaqli, “dotard of mind” (from kharifa, to become senile), or al-khafīf al-ʿaqli, “light of mind, feather-brained”; either way the cub is calling the donkey a fool. The print is kept and pointed as it stands.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ يَا ابْنَ السُّلْطَانِ أَنَا جِنْسِي حِمَارٌ وَسَبَبُ قُدُومِي إِلَى هَذَا الْمَكَانِ هُرُوبِي مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu yā ibna al-sulṭāni anā jinsī ḥimārun wa-sababu qudūmī ilā hādhā al-makāni hurūbī mini ibni Ādama
sentences.l: And he said to him: O son of the sultan, I, my kind (is) donkey, and the cause of my coming to this place (is) my fleeing from the Son of Adam.
sentences.i: He said to him, “O son of the sultan, I am a donkey by kind, and what brings me here is that I am fleeing from the Son of Adam.”
sentences.n: The print has السطان, a misprint for السلطان, corrected here. anā jinsī ḥimār, “I, my kind is donkey”: the topic is set first and then commented on, a common spoken pattern. hurūb, “flight”, is the spoken verbal noun of haraba beside the classical harab.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الشِّبْلُ وَهَلْ أَنْتَ خَائِفٌ مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ أَنْ يَقْتُلَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-shiblu wa-hal anta khāʾifun mini ibni Ādama an yaqtulaka
sentences.l: And the cub said to him: And are you afraid of the Son of Adam, that he kill you?
sentences.i: The cub said to him, “Then are you afraid the Son of Adam will kill you?”
sentences.n: The hamza in خائف is the print's.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْحِمَارُ لَا يَابْنَ السُّلْطَانِ وَإِنَّمَا خَوْفِي أَنْ يَعْمَلَ حِيلَةً عَلَيَّ وَيَرْكَبَنِي لِأَنَّ عِنْدَهُ شَيْأً يُسَمِّيهِ الْبَرْذَعَةَ فَيَجْعَلُهَا عَلَى ظَهْرِي وَشَيْأً يُسَمِّيهِ الْحِزَامَ فَيَشُدُّهُ عَلَى بَطْنِي وَشَيْأً يُسَمِّيهِ الطَّفَرَ فَيَجْعَلُهُ تَحْتَ ذَنَبِي وَشَيْأً يُسَمِّيهِ اللِّجَامَ فَيَجْعَلُهُ فِي فَمِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-ḥimāru lā yā-bna al-sulṭāni wa-innamā khawfī an yaʿmala ḥīlatan ʿalayya wa-yarkabanī li-anna ʿindahu shayʾan yusammīhi al-bardhaʿata fa-yajʿaluhā ʿalā ẓahrī wa-shayʾan yusammīhi al-ḥizāma fa-yashudduhu ʿalā baṭnī wa-shayʾan yusammīhi al-ṭafara fa-yajʿaluhu taḥta dhanabī wa-shayʾan yusammīhi al-lijāma fa-yajʿaluhu fī famī
sentences.l: And the donkey said to him: No, O son of the sultan, but rather my fear (is) that he work a trick upon me and ride me; because with him (is) a thing he calls it the pack-saddle, and he puts it on my back, and a thing he calls it the girth, and he binds it on my belly, and a thing he calls it the crupper, and he puts it under my tail, and a thing he calls it the bridle, and he puts it in my mouth.
sentences.i: The donkey said to him, “No, son of the sultan. What I fear is that he will play some trick on me and ride me. For he has a thing he calls the pack-saddle, which he puts on my back; and a thing he calls the girth, which he binds round my belly; and a thing he calls the crupper, which he sets under my tail; and a thing he calls the bridle, which he puts in my mouth.
sentences.n: يابن, yā-bna, is run together in the print, yā plus ibn with its alif dropped; the spacing is kept. The shadda in عليّ is the print's. ʿamila ḥīlatan ʿalā, “to work a trick on”. شيأ is the print's spelling of shayʾan, kept. The list is built as a refrain, shayʾan yusammīhi … fa-yajʿaluhu, “a thing he calls … and he puts it”: the donkey speaks of the gear as strange contraptions he can only name by man's words. bardhaʿa, the padded pack-saddle of a donkey. al-ṭafar is doubtful: the strap that passes under the tail is in classical Arabic the thafar, “crupper”, and ṭafar is most likely a spoken or misprinted form of that word; the print is kept.

sentences.t: وَيَعْمَلُ لِي مِنْخَاسًا يَنْخَسُنِي بِهِ وَيُكَلِّفُنِي مَا لَا أُطِيقُ مِنَ الْجَرْيِ وَإِذَا عَثَرْتُ لَعَنَنِي وَإِنْ نَهَقْتُ شَتَمَنِي
sentences.tr: wa-yaʿmalu lī minkhāsan yankhasunī bihi wa-yukallifunī mā lā uṭīqu mina al-jaryi wa-idhā ʿathartu laʿananī wa-in nahaqtu shatamanī
sentences.l: And he makes for me a goad (that) he goads me with it, and he burdens me with what I cannot bear of the running; and if I stumble he curses me, and if I bray he reviles me.
sentences.i: He makes himself a goad to prod me with, and he forces more running on me than I can bear; if I stumble he curses me, and if I bray he abuses me.
sentences.n: minkhās, “goad”, from nakhasa, “to prod”: tool-noun and verb side by side, minkhāsan yankhasunī. kallafa, “to charge someone with (a burden)”. The last two clauses rhyme: laʿananī / shatamanī.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ إِذَا كَبِرْتُ وَ لَمْ أَقْدِرْ عَلَى الْجَرْيِ يَجْعَلُ لِي رَحْلًا مِنَ الْخَشَبِ وَيُسَلِّمُنِي إِلَى السَّقَّايِينَ فَيَحْمِلُونَ الْمَاءَ عَلَى ظَهْرِي مِنَ الْبَحْرِ فِى الْقِرَبِ وَنَحْوِهَا كَالْجِرَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika idhā kabirtu wa lam aqdir ʿalā al-jaryi yajʿalu lī raḥlan mina al-khashabi wa-yusallimunī ilā al-saqqāyīna fa-yaḥmilūna al-māʾa ʿalā ẓahrī mina al-baḥri fī al-qirabi wa-naḥwihā ka-al-jirāri
sentences.l: And after that, when I grow-old and am not able for the running, he makes for me a saddle of the wood and hands me over to the water-carriers, and they carry the water on my back from the river in the waterskins and the like-of-them, such-as the jars.
sentences.i: And later, when I grow old and can no longer run, he fits me with a wooden saddle and hands me over to the water-carriers, and they load my back with water from the river in skins and the like, such as jars.
sentences.n: The print sets و apart from لم; the spacing is kept. The kasras in القِرَب and كالجِرار are the print's, as is ى in فى. raḥl, a saddle, here a wooden frame for loads. saqqāyīn, “water-carriers”, is the spoken plural of saqqāʾ, with y where the classical form has hamza (saqqāʾūn). baḥr, usually “sea”, is in Egyptian usage also the Nile, the river.

sentences.t: وَلَا أَزَالُ فِي ذُلٍّ وَهَوَانٍ وَتَعَبٍ حَتَّى أَمُوتَ فَيَرْمُونَنِي فَوْقَ التِّلَالِ لِلْكِلَابِ
sentences.tr: wa-lā azālu fī dhullin wa-hawānin wa-taʿabin ḥattā amūta fa-yarmūnanī fawqa al-tilāli li-al-kilābi
sentences.l: And I do not cease (to be) in abasement and contempt and toil until I die, and they throw me upon the mounds for the dogs.
sentences.i: And so I live on in abasement, contempt and toil until I die, and then they throw me out on the rubbish mounds for the dogs.
sentences.n: lā azālu, “I do not cease”, here with a phrase, “I remain in”. tilāl, “hills, mounds”: the refuse heaps outside a town, where dead animals were thrown.

sentences.t: فَأَيُّ شَيْءٍ أَكْبَرُ مِنْ هَذَا الْهَمِّ وَأَيُّ مُصِيبَةٍ أَكْبَرُ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْمَصَائِبِ
sentences.tr: fa-ayyu shayʾin akbaru min hādhā al-hammi wa-ayyu muṣībatin akbaru min hādhihi al-maṣāʾibi
sentences.l: So what thing (is) greater than this grief, and what calamity (is) greater than these calamities?
sentences.i: What could be worse than this misery, and what calamity greater than these calamities?”
sentences.n: The shaddas in فايّ and وايّ are the print's; so is the hamza in المصائب.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ أَيُّهَا الطَّاؤُوسَةُ كَلَامَ الْحِمَارِ اقْشَعَرَّ جَسَدِي مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ وَقُلْتُ لِلشِّبْلِ يَاسَيِّدِي إِنَّ الْحِمَارَ مَعْذُورٌ وَقَدْ زَادَنِي كَلَامُهُ رُعْبًا عَلَى رُعْبِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿtu ayyuhā al-ṭāʾūsatu kalāma al-ḥimāri iqshaʿarra jasadī mini ibni Ādama wa-qultu li-al-shibli yā sayyidī inna al-ḥimāra maʿdhūrun wa-qad zādanī kalāmuhu ruʿban ʿalā ruʿbī
sentences.l: And when I heard, O you peahen, the speech of the donkey, my body shuddered from the Son of Adam; and I said to the cub: O my lord, indeed the donkey (is) excused, and his speech has increased me terror upon my terror.
sentences.i: When I heard the donkey's words, peahen, my flesh crept at the thought of the Son of Adam, and I said to the cub, “My lord, the donkey cannot be blamed; his words have added terror to my terror.”
sentences.n: The ḍamma in سمعتُ and the shadda in اقشعرّ are the print's, as is the hamza in الطاؤوسة. ayyuhā al-ṭāʾūsatu: classical Arabic would use the feminine ayyatuhā before a feminine noun; the text keeps the one form. ṭāʾūsa, “peahen”, feminine of ṭāʾūs. iqshaʿarra, “to shudder, bristle”, of skin creeping with fear. ياسيدي is run together in the print; the spacing is kept. maʿdhūr, “excused”, one who has a good reason.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الشِّبْلُ لِلْحِمَارِ إِلَى أَيْنَ أَنْتَ سَائِرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-shiblu li-al-ḥimāri ilā ayna anta sāʾirun
sentences.l: And the cub said to the donkey: To where (are) you going?
sentences.i: The cub said to the donkey, “Where are you going?”
sentences.n: The hamza in سائر is the print's.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْحِمَارُ إِنِّي نَظَرْتُ ابْنَ آدَمَ قَبْلَ إِشْرَاقِ الشَّمْسِ مِنْ بَعِيدٍ فَفَرَرْتُ هَرَبًا مِنْهُ وَهَا أَنَا أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَنْطَلِقَ وَلَمْ أَزَلْ أَجْرِي مِنْ شِدَّةِ خَوْفِي مِنْهُ فَعَسَى أَجِدُ لِي مَوْضِعًا يَأْوِينِي مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ الْغَدَّارِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-ḥimāru innī naẓartu ibna Ādama qabla ishrāqi al-shamsi min baʿīdin fa-farartu haraban minhu wa-hā anā urīdu an anṭaliqa wa-lam azal ajrī min shiddati khawfī minhu fa-ʿasā ajidu lī mawḍiʿan yaʾwīnī mini ibni Ādama al-ghaddāri
sentences.l: And the donkey said to him: Indeed I saw the Son of Adam before the rising of the sun from afar, and I fled in-flight from him; and here I (am) wanting that I go-off, and I have not ceased running from the severity of my fear of him, so perhaps I find for myself a place (that) shelters me from the Son of Adam, the treacherous.
sentences.i: The donkey said to him, “I caught sight of the Son of Adam from far off before sunrise and ran away from him, and now I mean to be off; I have been running ever since, I am so afraid of him, in the hope of finding some place that will shelter me from the treacherous Son of Adam.”
sentences.n: naẓara, “to look at”, here with a direct object, “to see”, as in spoken Arabic. farartu haraban, “I fled in flight”: the verbal noun of a near-synonym strengthens the verb. hā anā, “here I am”. ʿasā, “perhaps”, is followed directly by the verb, without an as the classical rule wants. The hamza in يأويني is the print's.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا ذَلِكَ الْحِمَارُ يَتَحَدَّثُ مَعَ الشِّبْلِ فِي ذَلِكَ الْكَلَامِ وَهُوَ يُرِيدُ أَنْ يُوَدِّعَنَا وَيَرُوحَ إِذْ ظَهَرَتْ لَنَا غَبْرَةٌ فَنَهَقَ الْحِمَارُ وَصَاحَ وَنَظَرَ بِعَيْنِهِ إِلَى نَاحِيَةِ الْغَبْرَةِ وَضَرَطَ ضُرَاطًا عَالِيًا
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā dhālika al-ḥimāru yataḥaddathu maʿa al-shibli fī dhālika al-kalāmi wa-huwa yurīdu an yuwaddiʿanā wa-yarūḥa idh ẓaharat lanā ghabratun fa-nahaqa al-ḥimāru wa-ṣāḥa wa-naẓara bi-ʿaynihi ilā nāḥiyati al-ghabrati wa-ḍaraṭa ḍurāṭan ʿāliyan
sentences.l: And while that donkey (was) talking with the cub in that speech, and he wanting that he bid-us-farewell and go, lo there appeared to us a dust; and the donkey brayed and shouted and looked with his eye toward the side of the dust, and farted a loud fart.
sentences.i: While the donkey was talking this way with the cub, and was about to take his leave of us and go, a cloud of dust appeared before us. The donkey brayed and cried out, stared toward the dust, and let out a loud fart.
sentences.n: baynamā … idh, “while … lo”, the narrator's frame for a sudden event. waddaʿa, “to bid farewell to”. rāḥa, “to go”. ḍaraṭa ḍurāṭan, “to fart a fart”, verb and its own verbal noun, here from fright.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ سَاعَةٍ انْكَشَفَتِ الْغَبْرَةُ عَنْ فَرَسٍ أَدْهَمَ بِغُرَّةٍ كَالدِّرْهَمِ وَذَلِكَ الْفَرَسُ ظَرِيفُ الْغُرَّةِ مَلِيحُ التَّحْجِيلِ حَسَنُ الْقَوَائِمِ وَالصَّهِيلِ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ يَجْرِي حَتَّى وَقَفَ بَيْنَ يَدَىِ الشِّبْلِ ابْنِ الْأَسَدِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda sāʿatin inkashafati al-ghabratu ʿan farasin adhama bi-ghurratin ka-al-dirhami wa-dhālika al-farasu ẓarīfu al-ghurrati malīḥu al-taḥjīli ḥasanu al-qawāʾimi wa-al-ṣahīli wa-lam yazal yajrī ḥattā waqafa bayna yadayi al-shibli ibni al-asadi
sentences.l: And after an hour the dust uncovered-itself from a horse, black, with a blaze like the dirham; and that horse (was) elegant of the blaze, handsome of the stockings, fine of the legs and the neighing; and he did not cease running until he stood between the two-hands of the cub, son of the lion.
sentences.i: After a while the dust lifted from a jet-black horse with a blaze like a silver coin, a horse with an elegant blaze and handsome white stockings, fine in the legs and fine in his neighing. He ran on until he halted before the cub, the lion's son.
sentences.n: adham, “black”, of a horse. ghurra, the white blaze on a horse's forehead; dirham, the silver coin, to which it is likened. taḥjīl, the white markings on a horse's legs, its “stockings”. The construction ẓarīfu al-ghurrati, “elegant of the blaze”, is the adjective followed by the part praised. The hamza in القوائم is the print's; يدى is written with ى, pointed yadayi before the article. sāʿa, “hour”, often just “a while”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأٰهُ الشِّبْلُ اسْتَعْظَمَهُ وَقَالَ لَهُ مَا جِنْسُكَ أَيُّهَا الْوَحْشُ الْجَلِيلُ وَمَا سَبَبُ شُرُودِكَ فِي هَذَا الْبَرِّ الْعَرِيضِ الطَّوِيلِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhu al-shiblu istaʿẓamahu wa-qāla lahu mā jinsuka ayyuhā al-waḥshu al-jalīlu wa-mā sababu shurūdika fī hādhā al-barri al-ʿarīḍi al-ṭawīli
sentences.l: And when the cub saw him, he thought-him-mighty and said to him: What (is) your kind, O you majestic beast, and what (is) the cause of your running-loose in this open-country, the broad, the long?
sentences.i: When the cub saw him he was awed by his size and said to him, “What kind of creature are you, majestic beast, and why are you running wild in this wide and endless wilderness?”
sentences.n: رأه again for raʾāhu. istaʿẓama, “to deem great”. shurūd, “running away, straying”, of an animal. barr, “open land, the wilds” as opposed to settled country. The cub's question rhymes: al-jalīl / al-ṭawīl.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ يَاسَيِّدَ الْوُحُوشِ أَنَا فَرَسٌ مِنْ جِنْسِ الْخَيْلِ وَسَبَبُ شُرُودِى هُرُوبِي مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu yā sayyida al-wuḥūshi anā farasun min jinsi al-khayli wa-sababu shurūdī hurūbī mini ibni Ādama
sentences.l: And he said to him: O lord of the beasts, I (am) a horse of the kind of the horses, and the cause of my running-loose (is) my fleeing from the Son of Adam.
sentences.i: He said to him, “Lord of the beasts, I am a horse, of the race of horses, and I am running wild because I am fleeing from the Son of Adam.”
sentences.n: ياسيد is run together in the print, and شرودى is written with ى; both are kept. The horse's answer echoes the donkey's word for word.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ الشِّبْلُ مِنْ كَلَامِ الْفَرَسِ وَقَالَ لَهُ لَا تَقُلْ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ فَإِنَّهُ عَيْبٌ عَلَيْكَ وَأَنْتَ طَوِيلٌ غَلِيظٌ وَكَيْفَ تَخَافُ مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ مَعَ عِظَمِ جُثَّتِكَ وَسُرْعَةِ جَرْيِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba al-shiblu min kalāmi al-farasi wa-qāla lahu lā taqul hādhā al-kalāma fa-innahu ʿaybun ʿalayka wa-anta ṭawīlun ghalīẓun wa-kayfa takhāfu mini ibni Ādama maʿa ʿiẓami juththatika wa-surʿati jaryika
sentences.l: And the cub marvelled at the speech of the horse and said to him: Do not say this speech, for it (is) a shame upon you, and you (are) tall, thick; and how do you fear the Son of Adam, with the greatness of your bulk and the swiftness of your running?
sentences.i: The cub was astonished at the horse's words and said to him, “Do not say such a thing; it is a disgrace to you, tall and massive as you are. How can you be afraid of the Son of Adam, with your great bulk and your swiftness?
sentences.n: ʿayb ʿalayka, “a shame upon you”, still the everyday way of saying “shame on you”. wa-anta ṭawīl, “and you are tall”: a circumstantial clause, “when you are”. juththa, “body, bulk”.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا مَعَ صِغَرِ جِسْمِي قَدْ عَزَمْتُ عَلَى أَنْ أَلْتَقِيَ مَعَ ابْنِ آدَمَ فَأَبْطِشَ بِهِ وَآكُلَ لَحْمَهُ وَأُسَكِّنَ رَوْعَ هَذِهِ الْبَطَّةِ الْمِسْكِينَةِ وَأُقِرَّهَا فِي وَطَنِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-anā maʿa ṣighari jismī qad ʿazamtu ʿalā an altaqiya maʿa ibni Ādama fa-abṭisha bihi wa-ākula laḥmahu wa-usakkina rawʿa hādhihi al-baṭṭati al-miskīnati wa-uqirrahā fī waṭanihā
sentences.l: And I, with the smallness of my body, have resolved upon that I meet with the Son of Adam, and assault him, and eat his flesh, and calm the fright of this poor duck, and settle-her in her homeland.
sentences.i: Small as I am, I have made up my mind to meet the Son of Adam, fall upon him and eat his flesh, and so quiet the fears of this poor duck and let her live at peace in her own home.
sentences.n: ʿazama ʿalā, “to resolve on”. iltaqā maʿa, “to meet with”. baṭasha bi-, “to seize violently, fall upon”: the verb takes bi-. After an the verbs run on in the subjunctive: altaqiya, abṭisha, ākula, usakkina, uqirrahā. rawʿ, “fright”. aqarra, “to make settled, let stay”. The madda in وآكل is the print's.

sentences.t: وَهَا أَنْتَ لَمَّا أَتَيْتَ فِي هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ قَطَعْتَ قَلْبِي بِكَلَامِكَ وَأَرْجَعْتَنِي عَمَّا أَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَفْعَلَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-hā anta lammā atayta fī hādhihi al-sāʿati qaṭaʿta qalbī bi-kalāmika wa-arjaʿtanī ʿammā aradtu an afʿalahu
sentences.l: And here you, when you came in this hour, you cut my heart with your speech and made-me-turn-back from what I wanted that I do it.
sentences.i: And now you, coming along at this moment, have cut my courage short with your talk and turned me back from what I meant to do.
sentences.n: qaṭaʿa qalbahu, “to cut someone's heart”, to dishearten. arjaʿa, “to make return”: the causative of rajaʿa, standard in spoken Arabic where the classical language prefers rajaʿa itself or radda.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا كُنْتَ أَنْتَ مَعَ عِظَمِكَ قَدْ قَهَرَكَ ابْنُ آدَمَ وَلَمْ يَخَفْ مِنْ طُولِكَ وَعَرْضِكَ مَعَ أَنَّكَ لَوْ رَفَصْتَهُ بِرِجْلِكَ لَقَتَلْتَهُ وَلَمْ يَقْدِرْ عَلَيْكَ بَلْ تَسْقِيهِ كَأْسَ الرَّدَى
sentences.tr: fa-idhā kunta anta maʿa ʿiẓamika qad qaharaka ibnu Ādama wa-lam yakhaf min ṭūlika wa-ʿarḍika maʿa annaka law rafaṣtahu bi-rijlika la-qataltahu wa-lam yaqdir ʿalayka bal tasqīhi kaʾsa al-radā
sentences.l: So if you were, you, with your greatness, the Son of Adam has overpowered you and not feared from your length and your breadth, although you, if you kicked him with your foot, you would-kill him, and he would not have-power over you, but rather you would give-him-to-drink the cup of the death,
sentences.i: So if you, for all your size, have been mastered by the Son of Adam, and he was not afraid of your height and breadth, when one kick of your hoof would kill him and he could do nothing against you, but you would make him drink the cup of death—”
sentences.n: The “if” clause never reaches its main clause: the cub breaks off, and the narrative resumes with the horse’s laughter. rafaṣa, “to kick”, the spoken word for classical rakaḍa or rafasa. law … la-qataltahu, “if … you would have killed him”. kās, “cup”, is printed without its hamza (كاس for كأس); the hamza is supplied in the pointing. al-radā, “ruin, death”: “to make someone drink the cup of death” is a stock phrase of poetry and rhymed prose.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَ الْفَرَسُ لَمَّا سَمِعَ كَلَامَ الشِّبْلِ وَقَالَ هَيْهَاتَ هَيْهَاتَ أَنْ أَغْلِبَهُ يَا ابْنَ الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥika al-farasu lammā samiʿa kalāma al-shibli wa-qāla hayhāta hayhāta an aghlibahu yā ibna al-maliki
sentences.l: And the horse laughed when he heard the speech of the cub, and said: Far-off, far-off (is it) that I overcome him, O son of the king!
sentences.i: The horse laughed when he heard the cub's words and said, “Far from it, far from it, that I should get the better of him, O king's son!”
sentences.n: The print has با ابن, a misprint for يا ابن, corrected here: the print’s بـ has one dot where the vocative yā has two. hayhāta, “how far!”, says that a thing is out of all reach; hayhāta an aghlibahu, “far from it that I should overcome him”. The cub is the son of the lion, “sultan of the beasts”, so the animals address him as son of the king or son of the sultan.

sentences.t: فَلَا يَغُرَّكَ طُولِي وَلَا عَرْضِي وَلَا ضَخَامَتِي مَعَ ابْنِ آدَمَ
sentences.tr: fa-lā yaghurraka ṭūlī wa-lā ʿarḍī wa-lā ḍakhāmatī maʿa ibni Ādama
sentences.l: So let not deceive-you my length nor my breadth nor my bulk, with the Son of Adam.
sentences.i: “So do not be deceived by my height or my breadth or my bulk where the Son of Adam is concerned.
sentences.n: lā yaghurraka, “let it not deceive you”: lā with the jussive is a prohibition, and the doubled verb gharra takes the form yaghurra. maʿa, “with”, here “in dealing with, against”.

sentences.t: لِأَنَّهُ مِنْ شِدَّةِ حِيَلِهِ وَمَكْرِهِ يَصْنَعُ لِي شَيْأً يُقَالُ لَهُ الشِّكَالُ وَيَضَعُ فِي أَرْبَعَةِ قَوَائِمِي شِكَالَيْنِ مِنْ حِبَالِ اللِّيفِ الْمَلْفُوفَةِ بِاللِّبَادِ
sentences.tr: li-annahu min shiddati ḥiyalihi wa-makrihi yaṣnaʿu lī shayʾan yuqālu lahu al-shikālu wa-yaḍaʿu fī arbaʿati qawāʾimī shikālayni min ḥibāli al-līfi al-malfūfati bi-al-libādi
sentences.l: Because he, from the strength of his tricks and his cunning, makes for me a thing which is-called the hobble, and puts on four of my legs two-hobbles of ropes of palm-fibre, the (ones) wrapped with felt.
sentences.i: For he is so full of tricks and cunning that he makes for me a thing called a hobble, and on my four legs he puts two hobbles of palm-fibre rope wrapped in felt.
sentences.n: shikāl, “hobble”, a rope tying a horse's legs together so it cannot run; two of them bind the four legs in pairs. līf, the fibre of the date palm, the common rope-stuff; libād, felt, wrapped round it so that it does not chafe. arbaʿati qawāʾimī, “four of my legs”, is a loose construct for “my four legs”. شيأ is the print's spelling of shayʾan; the hamza in قوائمي is the print's.

sentences.t: وَيَصْلُبُنِي مِنْ رَأْسِي فِي وَتَدٍ عَالٍ وَأَبْقَى وَاقِفًا وَأَنَا مَصْلُوبٌ لَا أَقْدِرُ أَقْعُدُ وَلَا أَنَامُ
sentences.tr: wa-yaṣlubunī min raʾsī fī watadin ʿālin wa-abqā wāqifan wa-anā maṣlūbun lā aqdiru aqʿudu wa-lā anāmu
sentences.l: And he strings-me-up by my head to a high peg, and I remain standing, and I (am) strung-up; I cannot sit nor sleep.
sentences.i: He ties me up by the head to a high peg, and there I stay standing, strung up, unable to lie down or sleep.
sentences.n: ṣalaba, properly “to crucify”, is used here of tying the horse's head up short to a tall stake. lā aqdiru aqʿudu, “I cannot sit”: the second verb follows directly in the indicative, without the an of Classical Arabic, a spoken construction. ʿālin, “high”, is ʿālī with the final -ī dropped in the indefinite. The hamza in رأسي is the print's.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا أَرَادَ أَنْ يَرْكَبَنِي يَعْمَلُ لِي شَيْأً فِي رِجْلَيْهِ مِنَ الْحَدِيدِ اسْمُهُ الرِّكَابُ وَيَضَعُ عَلَى ظَهْرِي شَيْأً يُسَمِّيهِ السَّرْجَ وَيَشُدُّهُ بِحِزَامَيْنِ مِنْ تَحْتِ إِبْطِي
sentences.tr: wa-idhā arāda an yarkabanī yaʿmalu lī shayʾan fī rijlayhi mina al-ḥadīdi ismuhu al-rikābu wa-yaḍaʿu ʿalā ẓahrī shayʾan yusammīhi al-sarja wa-yashudduhu bi-ḥizāmayni min taḥti ibṭī
sentences.l: And when he wants to ride me, he makes for me a thing for his two-feet of iron, its name the stirrup, and puts on my back a thing he calls the saddle, and fastens-it with two-girths from under my armpit.
sentences.i: When he wants to ride me he makes himself a thing of iron for his feet, called a stirrup, and on my back he puts a thing he calls a saddle, and he straps it on with two girths under my belly.
sentences.n: The print has ويشدة, a misprint for ويشده, corrected here: the pronoun -hu on the verb was set with the dots of a tāʾ marbūṭa. The horse describes tack as though seeing it for the first time, naming each piece: “a thing he calls the saddle”. ʿamala, “to do, make”, is the everyday verb for “make” here. rikāb, “stirrup”; sarj, “saddle”; ḥizām, “girth”; ibṭ, “armpit”, of the horse the hollow behind the forelegs.

sentences.t: وَيَضَعُ فِي فَمِي شَيْأً مِنَ الْحَدِيدِ يُسَمِّيهِ اللِّجَامَ وَيَضَعُ فِيهِ شَيْأً مِنَ الْجِلْدِ يُسَمِّيهِ الصَّرْعَ
sentences.tr: wa-yaḍaʿu fī famī shayʾan mina al-ḥadīdi yusammīhi al-lijāma wa-yaḍaʿu fīhi shayʾan mina al-jildi yusammīhi al-ṣarʿa
sentences.l: And he puts in my mouth a thing of iron he calls the bridle, and he puts on it a thing of leather he calls the ṣarʿ.
sentences.i: He puts in my mouth a thing of iron he calls a bridle, and fastens to it a thing of leather he calls the rein.
sentences.n: lijām, “bridle”, here the iron bit. الصرع is plainly the leather rein, which the rider holds in his hand in the next sentence, but the word is not the usual one (ʿinān) and its form is uncertain: it may be a colloquial term, or a misprint for a word such as سرع. It is kept as printed and pointed ṣarʿ only as a guess.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا رَكِبَ فَوْقَ ظَهْرِى عَلَى السَّرْجِ يُمْسِكُ الصَّرْعَ بِيَدِهِ وَيَقُودُنِي بِهِ وَيَهْمِزُنِي بِالرِّكَابِ فِي خَوَاصِرِي حَتَّى يُدْمِيَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-idhā rakiba fawqa ẓahrī ʿalā al-sarji yumsiku al-ṣarʿa bi-yadihi wa-yaqūdunī bihi wa-yahmizunī bi-al-rikābi fī khawāṣirī ḥattā yudmiyahā
sentences.l: And when he rides above my back on the saddle, he holds the rein with his hand and leads me by it, and goads me with the stirrup in my flanks until he makes-them-bleed.
sentences.i: Once he is up on my back in the saddle, he holds the rein in his hand and steers me with it, and spurs me in the flanks with the stirrup until they bleed.
sentences.n: hamaza, “to goad, spur”: Arab stirrups had sharp edges that served as spurs. khawāṣir, plural of khāṣira, “flank”. adamā, “to make bleed”. The print writes ظهرى with final ى.

sentences.t: وَلَا تَسْأَلْ يَا ابْنَ السُّلْطَانِ عَنْ مَا أُقَاسِيهِ مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ
sentences.tr: wa-lā tasʾal yā ibna al-sulṭāni ʿan mā uqāsīhi mini ibni Ādama
sentences.l: And do not ask, O son of the sultan, about what I suffer from the Son of Adam.
sentences.i: And do not ask, O son of the sultan, what I endure at the hands of the Son of Adam.
sentences.n: lā tasʾal ʿan, “do not ask about”, an idiom for “it is past telling”. qāsā, “to suffer, endure”. The print sets ʿan mā as two words, where Classical spelling joins them as عمّا.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا كَبِرْتُ وَانْتَحَلَ ظَهْرِى وَلَمْ أَقْدِرْ عَلَى سُرْعَةِ الْجَرْىِ يَبِيعُنِي لِلطَّحَّانِ لِيُدَوِّرَنِي فِى الطَّاحُونِ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā kabirtu wa-intaḥala ẓahrī wa-lam aqdir ʿalā surʿati al-jaryi yabīʿunī li-al-ṭaḥḥāni li-yudawwiranī fī al-ṭāḥūni
sentences.l: And when I grow-old and my back wastes-away and I cannot (manage) the swiftness of running, he sells me to the miller, so-that he may turn-me-round in the mill.
sentences.i: When I grow old and my back wears thin and I can no longer run fast, he sells me to the miller to turn the mill-wheel.
sentences.n: intaḥala usually means “to claim falsely”, which makes no sense here; the horse seems to mean that his back has grown thin and worn, as with naḥala, “to become emaciated”, or perhaps inḥalla, “to give way”. The reading is doubtful; the print's word is kept. yudawwiranī, “make me go round”: the horse walks in a circle to turn the millstone. The shadda in الطحّان is the print's.

sentences.t: فَلَا أَزَالُ دَائِرًا فِيهَا لَيْلًا وَنَهَارًا إِلَى أَنْ أَهْرَمَ فَيَبِيعُنِي لِلْجَزَّارِ فَيَذْبَحُنِي وَيَسْلُخُ جِلْدِى وَيَنْتِفُ ذَنَبِي وَيَبِيعُهُمَا لِلْغَرَابِلِيِّ وَالْمَنَاخِلِيِّ وَيَسْلِي شَحْمِي
sentences.tr: fa-lā azālu dāʾiran fīhā laylan wa-nahāran ilā an ahrama fa-yabīʿunī li-al-jazzāri fa-yadhbaḥunī wa-yaslukhu jildī wa-yantifu dhanabī wa-yabīʿuhumā li-al-gharābiliyyi wa-al-manākhiliyyi wa-yaslī shaḥmī
sentences.l: And I do not cease going-round in it night and day until I grow-decrepit; then he sells me to the butcher, and he slaughters me and flays my hide and plucks my tail and sells them-two to the sieve-maker and the sifter-maker, and renders my fat.
sentences.i: There I go round and round night and day until I am worn out with age, and then he sells me to the butcher, who slaughters me, strips off my hide, plucks out my tail, sells the two to the makers of sieves and sifters, and renders down my fat.”
sentences.n: fīhā, “in it”, treats al-ṭāḥūn, the mill, as feminine. harima, “to become decrepit with age”. The hide made the base of a sieve and the tail-hair the fine mesh of a sifter: gharābilī and manākhilī are trade names formed from the plurals gharābil, “sieves”, and manākhil, “sifters”. yaslī, “he renders”, is taken from salaʾa, “to clarify fat or butter”, with the hamza lost, as in speech; the reading is likely but not certain. The hamza in دائرا is the print's; جلدى is written with final ى.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الشِّبْلُ كَلَامَ الْفَرَسِ ازْدَادَ غَيْظًا وَغَمًّا وَقَالَ لَهُ مَتَى فَارَقْتَ ابْنَ آدَمَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-shiblu kalāma al-farasi izdāda ghayẓan wa-ghamman wa-qāla lahu matā fāraqta ibna Ādama
sentences.l: And when the cub heard the speech of the horse, he increased (in) rage and grief, and said to him: When did you part from the Son of Adam?
sentences.i: When the cub heard what the horse said, his anger and distress grew, and he asked him, “When did you leave the Son of Adam?”
sentences.n: The print has غظيا, a misprint for غيظا, corrected here: the yāʾ and ẓāʾ were set in the wrong order. izdāda ghayẓan wa-ghamman, “he increased in rage and grief”: the nouns are accusatives of specification.

sentences.t: قَالَ فَارَقْتُهُ نِصْفَ النَّهَارِ وَهُوَ فِي أَثَرِي
sentences.tr: qāla fāraqtuhu niṣfa al-nahāri wa-huwa fī atharī
sentences.l: He said: I parted-from-him (at) the half of the day, and he (is) on my track.
sentences.i: He said, “I left him at midday, and he is on my trail.”
sentences.n: fī atharī, “on my track, close behind me”.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا الشِّبْلُ يَتَحَدَّثُ مَعَ الْفَرَسِ فِي هَذَا الْكَلَامِ وَإِذَا بِغَبْرَةٍ ثَارَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā al-shiblu yataḥaddathu maʿa al-farasi fī hādhā al-kalāmi wa-idhā bi-ghabratin thārat
sentences.l: And while the cub was talking with the horse in this speech, and behold, a dust-cloud rose.
sentences.i: While the cub was still talking with the horse, a cloud of dust suddenly rose up.
sentences.n: baynamā … wa-idhā bi-, “while … behold”: the stock frame for a sudden event, the bi- only marking what appears. ghabara, “cloud of dust”, the usual sign in the Nights that someone is coming.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ انْكَشَفَتِ الْغَبْرَةُ وَبَانَ مِنْ تَحْتِهَا جَمَلٌ هَائِجٌ وَهُوَ يُبَعْبِعُ وَيَخْبِطُ بِرِجْلَيْهِ فِى الْأَرْضِ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ يَفْعَلُ كَذَلِكَ حَتَّى وَصَلَ إِلَيْنَا
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika inkashafati al-ghabratu wa-bāna min taḥtihā jamalun hāʾijun wa-huwa yubaʿbiʿu wa-yakhbiṭu bi-rijlayhi fī al-arḍi wa-lam yazal yafʿalu ka-dhālika ḥattā waṣala ilaynā
sentences.l: And after that the dust-cloud cleared, and there appeared from under it a camel, raging, and he (was) bellowing and stamping with his two-feet on the ground, and he did not cease doing thus until he reached us.
sentences.i: Then the dust cleared, and out of it appeared a camel in a frenzy, bellowing and stamping the ground, and on he came like that until he reached us.
sentences.n: hāʾij, “agitated, in a frenzy”; the hamza is the print's. baʿbaʿa, a sound-word for a camel's gurgling roar. ilaynā, “to us”: the duck is telling the story, and she was there with the cub.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأٰهُ الشِّبْلُ كَبِيرًا غَلِيظًا ظَنَّ أَنَّهُ ابْنُ آدَمَ فَأَرَادَ الْوُثُوبَ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhu al-shiblu kabīran ghalīẓan ẓanna annahu ibnu Ādama fa-arāda al-wuthūba ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And when the cub saw him big, thick, he thought that he was the Son of Adam, and he wanted the leaping upon him.
sentences.i: When the cub saw how big and massive he was, he took him for the Son of Adam and made to spring on him.
sentences.n: The print spells raʾāhu as رأه, without the madda; it is pointed here with a small alif. kabīran ghalīẓan, “big, thick”, describes the camel as the cub saw him. wathaba ʿalā, “to leap upon”, of a beast of prey.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُ يَا ابْنَ السُّلْطَانِ إِنَّ هَذَا مَا هُوَ ابْنُ آدَمَ وَإِنَّمَا هَذَا جَمَلٌ وَكَأَنَّهُ هَارِبٌ مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahu yā ibna al-sulṭāni inna hādhā mā huwa ibnu Ādama wa-innamā hādhā jamalun wa-kaʾannahu hāribun mini ibni Ādama
sentences.l: And I said to him: O son of the sultan, indeed this, not is he the Son of Adam; rather this (is) a camel, and it-is-as-though he (is) fleeing from the Son of Adam.
sentences.i: I said to him, “Son of the sultan, this is not the Son of Adam, only a camel, and he seems to be running away from the Son of Adam himself.”
sentences.n: mā huwa, “it is not”: negation with mā and a pronoun, as in speech, where Classical Arabic would use laysa. The hamza in وكأنه is the print's.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا أَنَا يَا أُخْتِي مَعَ الشِّبْلِ فِي هَذَا الْكَلَامِ وَإِذَا بِالْجَمَلِ تَقَدَّمَ بَيْنَ أَيَادِى الشِّبْلِ وَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِ فَرَدَّ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامَ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā anā yā ukhtī maʿa al-shibli fī hādhā al-kalāmi wa-idhā bi-al-jamali taqaddama bayna ayādī al-shibli wa-sallama ʿalayhi fa-radda ʿalayhi al-salāma
sentences.l: And while I, O my sister, (was) with the cub in this speech, and behold, the camel came-forward between the hands of the cub and greeted him, and he returned the greeting to him.
sentences.i: While I was still talking with the cub, my sister, the camel came up before him and greeted him, and the cub returned his greeting.
sentences.n: yā ukhtī, “O my sister”: the duck turns to the peahen she is telling all this to. bayna ayādī, “between the hands of”, means “before, in the presence of”; ayādī, a plural of yad, is written with final ى. sallama ʿalā, “to greet”, by saying al-salām ʿalaykum; radda al-salām, “to return the greeting”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ مَا سَبَبُ مَجِيئِكَ فِي هَذَا الْمَكَانِ قَالَ جِئْتُ هَارِبًا مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu mā sababu majīʾika fī hādhā al-makāni qāla jiʾtu hāriban mini ibni Ādama
sentences.l: And he said to him: What (is) the reason of your coming in this place? He said: I came fleeing from the Son of Adam.
sentences.i: The cub said to him, “What brings you to this place?” He said, “I have come here running from the Son of Adam.”
sentences.n: fī hādhā al-makān, “in this place”, where Classical usage would say ilā, “to”. The hamza in مجيئك and in جئت is the print's.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الشِّبْلُ وَأَنْتَ مَعَ عِظَمِ خِلْقَتِكَ وَطُولِكَ وَعَرْضِكَ كَيْفَ تَخَافُ مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ وَلَوْ رَفَصْتَهُ بِرِجْلِكَ رَفْصَةً لَقَتَلْتَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-shiblu wa-anta maʿa ʿiẓami khilqatika wa-ṭūlika wa-ʿarḍika kayfa takhāfu mini ibni Ādama wa-law rafaṣtahu bi-rijlika rafṣatan la-qataltahu
sentences.l: And the cub said to him: And you, with the greatness of your frame and your length and your breadth, how do you fear the Son of Adam? And if you kicked-him with your foot one kick, you would-have-killed-him.
sentences.i: The cub said to him, “You, with that huge frame of yours, so tall and so broad, how can you be afraid of the Son of Adam? One kick of your foot would kill him.”
sentences.n: The print has واو رفصته, a misprint for ولو رفصته, corrected here: the lām of law was set as an alif, and the la- of la-qataltahu that answers it confirms the reading. rafaṣa, “to kick”, is a spoken form of the Classical rafasa; rafṣatan, “a single kick”, is an accusative of the noun of one act. khilqa, “frame, build”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْجَمَلُ يَا ابْنَ السُّلْطَانِ اعْلَمْ أَنَّ ابْنَ آدَمَ لَهُ دَوَاهِي لَاتُطَاقُ وَمَا يَغْلِبُهُ إِلَّا الْمَوْتُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-jamalu yā ibna al-sulṭāni iʿlam anna ibna Ādama lahu dawāhī lā tuṭāqu wa-mā yaghlibuhu illā al-mawtu
sentences.l: And the camel said to him: O son of the sultan, know that the Son of Adam, to him (are) calamities not-to-be-borne, and nothing overcomes him except death.
sentences.i: The camel said to him, “Son of the sultan, know that the Son of Adam has wiles past all bearing, and nothing gets the better of him but death.
sentences.n: dawāhī, plural of dāhiya, “calamity”, and also “cunning, a craft that brings ruin”, which is the sense here. Classical Arabic would write the indefinite plural دواه, dawāhin; the print keeps the final ي. The print runs lā tuṭāq, “not to be borne”, together as لاتطاق; the spacing is kept.

sentences.t: لِأَنَّهُ يَضَعُ فِي أَنْفِي خَيْطًا وَيُسَمِّيهِ خِزَامًا وَيَجْعَلُ فِي رَأْسِي مِقْوَدًا وَيُسَلِّمُنِي إِلَى أَصْغَرِ أَوْلَادِهِ فَيَجُرُّنِي الْوَلَدُ الصَّغِيرُ بِالْخَيْطِ مَعَ كِبَرِي وَعِظَمِي
sentences.tr: li-annahu yaḍaʿu fī anfī khayṭan wa-yusammīhi khizāman wa-yajʿalu fī raʾsī miqwadan wa-yusallimunī ilā aṣghari awlādihi fa-yajurrunī al-waladu al-ṣaghīru bi-al-khayṭi maʿa kibarī wa-ʿiẓamī
sentences.l: Because he puts in my nose a thread and calls-it a nose-ring, and he sets on my head a halter, and he hands-me-over to the smallest of his children, and the small boy drags me by the thread, with my bigness and my greatness.
sentences.i: For he puts a cord through my nose and calls it a nose-ring, and puts a halter on my head, and hands me over to the youngest of his children, and the little boy leads me along by the cord, big and mighty as I am.
sentences.n: khizām, the ring or cord through a camel's nose by which it is led. miqwad, “halter, leading-rope”. maʿa kibarī wa-ʿiẓamī, “with my size and greatness”, that is, for all my size. The shadda in فيجرّني is the print's; so is the hamza in رأسي.

sentences.t: وَيُحَمِّلُونَنِي أَثْقَلَ الْأَحْمَالِ وَيُسَافِرُونَ بِي الْأَسْفَارَ الطِّوَالَ وَيَسْتَعْمِلُونَنِي فِى الْأَشْغَالِ الشَّاقَّةِ آنَاءَ اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-yuḥammilūnanī athqala al-aḥmāli wa-yusāfirūna bī al-asfāra al-ṭiwāla wa-yastaʿmilūnanī fī al-ashghāli al-shāqqati ānāʾa al-layli wa-al-nahāri
sentences.l: And they load-me (with) the heaviest of the loads, and they journey with me the long journeys, and they employ-me in the hard tasks (in) the hours of the night and the day.
sentences.i: They load me with the heaviest burdens, take me on long journeys, and work me at hard labour all the hours of the night and the day.
sentences.n: The subject turns from “he” to “they”: the Son of Adam is now mankind at large. ānāʾa al-layli wa-al-nahār, “in the hours of night and day”, a Qurʾanic phrase; the madda and hamza of آناء are the print's.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا كَبِرْتُ وَشِخْتُ أَوِ انْكَسَرْتُ فَلَمْ يَحْفَظْ صُحْبَتِي بَلْ يَبِيعُنِي لِلْجَزَّارِ فَيَذْبَحُنِي وَيَبِيعُ جِلْدِي لِلدَّبَّاغِينَ وَلَحْمِى لِلطَّبَّاخِينَ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā kabirtu wa-shikhtu awi inkasartu fa-lam yaḥfaẓ ṣuḥbatī bal yabīʿunī li-al-jazzāri fa-yadhbaḥunī wa-yabīʿu jildī li-al-dabbāghīna wa-laḥmī li-al-ṭabbākhīna
sentences.l: And when I grow-big and grow-old or break-down, he does not keep my companionship, but sells me to the butcher, and he slaughters me and sells my hide to the tanners and my flesh to the cooks.
sentences.i: And when I grow old and grey, or break down, he keeps no faith with all the years I served him, but sells me to the butcher, who slaughters me and sells my hide to the tanners and my flesh to the cooks.
sentences.n: shikhtu, “I grew old”, from shākha, yashīkhu; the kasra on the shīn is the print's. lam yaḥfaẓ, past in form, here states what always happens. ḥafiẓa al-ṣuḥba, “to keep faith with companionship”, to honour long service. The print writes لحمى with final ى.

sentences.t: وَلَا تَسْأَلْ عَنْ مَا أُقَاسِي مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ
sentences.tr: wa-lā tasʾal ʿan mā uqāsī mini ibni Ādama
sentences.l: And do not ask about what I suffer from the Son of Adam.
sentences.i: And do not ask what I endure from the Son of Adam.”
sentences.n: The camel ends with the horse's very words, a refrain each beast repeats.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الشِّبْلُ أَيَّ وَقْتٍ فَارَقْتَ ابْنَ آدَمَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-shiblu ayya waqtin fāraqta ibna Ādama
sentences.l: And the cub said to him: What time did you part from the Son of Adam?
sentences.i: The cub asked him, “When did you leave the Son of Adam?”
sentences.n: The shadda in ايّ is the print's.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ فَارَقْتُهُ وَقْتَ الْغُرُوبِ وَأَظُنُّهُ يَأْتِي عِنْدَ انْصِرَافِي فَلَمْ يَجِدْنِي فَيَسْعَى فِي طَلَبِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla fāraqtuhu waqta al-ghurūbi wa-aẓunnuhu yaʾtī ʿinda inṣirāfī fa-lam yajidnī fa-yasʿā fī ṭalabī
sentences.l: And he said: I parted-from-him at the time of sunset, and I think-him (to be) coming at my going-away, and he did not find me, and he will go in search of me.
sentences.i: He said, “I left him at sunset, and I think he will have come by when I slipped away and not found me, and now he will be out looking for me.”
sentences.n: aẓunnuhu yaʾtī, “I think he comes”: the verb follows the pronoun directly, without anna. fa-lam yajidnī, past in form, is part of what the camel imagines has happened. The hamza in يأتي is the print's.

sentences.t: فَدَعْنِي يَا ابْنَ السُّلْطَانِ حَتَّى أَلْهَجَ فِى الْبَرَارِي وَالْقِفَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-daʿnī yā ibna al-sulṭāni ḥattā alhaja fī al-barārī wa-al-qifāri
sentences.l: So let-me-go, O son of the sultan, that I may roam in the wilds and the wastes.
sentences.i: So let me go, son of the sultan, and lose myself in the wilds and the wastes.
sentences.n: The print has البراي, a misprint for البراري, corrected here: one rāʾ was dropped. barārī and qifār, “open country and deserts”, a stock pair. الهج is doubtful: lahija means “to be given over to something”, which does not fit well, and the word may stand for ahijja, “to flee off at random”. It is kept as printed and translated from the sense.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الشِّبْلُ تَمَهَّلْ قَلِيلًا يَا جَمَلُ حَتَّى تَنْظُرَ كَيْفَ أَفْتَرِسُهُ وَأُطْعِمُكَ مِنْ لَحْمِهِ وَأَهْشِمُ عَظْمَهُ وَأَشْرَبُ مِنْ دَمِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-shiblu tamahhal qalīlan yā jamalu ḥattā tanẓura kayfa aftarisuhu wa-uṭʿimuka min laḥmihi wa-ahshimu ʿaẓmahu wa-ashrabu min damihi
sentences.l: And the cub said: Wait a little, O camel, until you see how I prey-upon-him, and feed you from his flesh, and crush his bone, and drink from his blood.
sentences.i: The cub said, “Wait a little, camel, and you will see how I make him my prey, and give you some of his flesh to eat, and crush his bones and drink his blood.”
sentences.n: iftarasa, “to seize and devour as prey”. The cub's offer to feed a camel on meat shows how little he knows. The shadda in تمهّل is the print's.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْجَمَلُ يَا ابْنَ السُّلْطَانِ أَنَا خَائِفٌ عَلَيْكَ مِنِ ابْنِ آدَمَ فَإِنَّهُ مُخَادِعٌ مَاكِرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-jamalu yā ibna al-sulṭāni anā khāʾifun ʿalayka mini ibni Ādama fa-innahu mukhādiʿun mākirun
sentences.l: And the camel said to him: O son of the sultan, I (am) fearing for you from the Son of Adam, for he (is) deceitful, cunning.
sentences.i: The camel said to him, “Son of the sultan, I fear for you from the Son of Adam, for he is a deceiver and full of guile.”
sentences.n: khāʾif ʿalā, “afraid for”. The hamza in خائف is the print's.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَنْشَدَ قَوْلَ الشَّاعِرِ
sentences.tr: thumma anshada qawla al-shāʿiri
sentences.l: Then he recited the saying of the poet:
sentences.i: Then he recited the poet's words:

sentences.t: اِذَا حَلَّ الثَّقِيْلُ باَرْضِ قَوْمٍ * فَمَا لِلسَّاكِنِيْنَ سِوَى الرَّحيْل
sentences.tr: idhā ḥalla al-thaqīlu bi-arḍi qawmin * fa-mā li-al-sākinīna siwā al-raḥīl
sentences.l: When the heavy-one alights in the land of a people, * then there is not for the dwellers (anything) but the departing.
sentences.i: When the oppressive one comes to settle in a people's land, * there is nothing left for those who live there but to leave.
sentences.n: The marks are the print's, including the sukūn on the long ī of al-thaqīl and al-sākinīn and the fatḥa set on the alif of باَرض. al-thaqīl, “the heavy one”, is the burdensome guest or overbearing neighbour whom no one can bear; the camel means the Son of Adam. The line ends in the pause on al-raḥīl, “departure”.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا الْجَمَلُ يَتَحَدَّثُ مَعَ الشِّبْلِ فِي هَذَا الْكَلَامِ وَإِذَا بِغَبْرَةٍ طَلَعَتْ وَبَعْدَ سَاعَةٍ انْكَشَفَتْ عَنْ شَيْخٍ قَصِيرٍ رَقِيقِ الْبَشَرَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā al-jamalu yataḥaddathu maʿa al-shibli fī hādhā al-kalāmi wa-idhā bi-ghabratin ṭalaʿat wa-baʿda sāʿatin inkashafat ʿan shaykhin qaṣīrin raqīqi al-basharati
sentences.l: And while the camel was-talking with the cub in this speech, and behold, a dust-cloud rose; and after an hour it uncovered (itself) from an old-man, short, thin of the skin.
sentences.i: While the camel was still talking with the cub in this way, a cloud of dust rose up, and after a while it cleared to show a short old man with thin skin.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”: the bi- only marks what suddenly appears. inkashafat ʿan, “it was lifted off (to reveal)”: the dust clears and shows what was inside it. sāʿa is “a while” as often as “an hour”. raqīq al-bashara, “thin of skin”: a frail, lean old man.

sentences.t: عَلَى كَتِفِهِ مِقْطَفٌ فِيهِ عُدَّةُ نَجَّارٍ وَعَلَى رَأْسِهِ شُعْبَةٌ وَثَمَانِيَةُ أَلْوَاحٍ وَبِيَدِهِ أَطْفَالٌ صِغَارٌ وَهُوَ يُهَرْوِلُ فِي مَشْيِهِ
sentences.tr: ʿalā katifihi miqṭafun fīhi ʿuddatu najjārin wa-ʿalā raʾsihi shuʿbatun wa-thamāniyatu alwāḥin wa-bi-yadihi aṭfālun ṣighārun wa-huwa yuharwilu fī mashyihi
sentences.l: On his shoulder a basket, in it the tools of a carpenter; and on his head a forked-branch and eight planks; and in his hand small children; and he was trotting in his walk.
sentences.i: On his shoulder was a basket holding a carpenter's tools, on his head a forked pole and eight planks, and by the hand he led little children; and he came along at a jog.
sentences.n: miqṭaf, “basket”, an Egyptian word for a palm-leaf basket. ʿuddat najjār, “a carpenter's gear”: this is the najjār, “carpenter”, of the tale's later running header. shuʿba is “a branch, a forked stick”; what exactly he carries is not clear. wa-bi-yadihi aṭfālun ṣighārun, “and in his hand small children”, is odd: perhaps he leads children by the hand, but the phrase may be corrupt, and no correction is certain. harwala, “to go at a jog-trot”, between walking and running. The shadda in عدّة and نجّار is the print's.

sentences.t: وَمَازَالَ يَمْشِي حَتَّى قَرُبَ مِنَ الشِّبْلِ
sentences.tr: wa-mā zāla yamshī ḥattā qaruba mina al-shibli
sentences.l: And he did-not-cease walking until he came-near to the cub.
sentences.i: He kept walking until he came near the cub.
sentences.n: The print runs mā zāla, “did not cease”, together as one word, ومازال; the spacing is kept.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُهُ يَا أُخْتِي وَقَعْتُ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الْخَوْفِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾaytuhu yā ukhtī waqaʿtu min shiddati al-khawfi
